blocks.content: Plain HTTP was built around a client asking a question and a server answering it, one request, one response, connection closed. That model breaks down the moment a server needs to tell a client something without being asked first, a chat message arriving, a price changing, a notification firing. Long polling and WebSockets are two different answers to that same problem, and choosing between them is a real, recurring system design decision.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396523086-609076097.png
blocks.alt: Short polling repeatedly asks the server whether anything new has happened, wasting most requests on a plain no

blocks.content: 1. The Problem: Getting Server Updates To A Client
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Getting Server Updates To A Client

blocks.content: A regular HTTP request is initiated by the client, and the server can only respond to that specific request, it cannot reach out on its own later and send something new. For anything that needs to feel live, a chat app, a live score, a collaborative document, the client somehow has to find out about server-side changes without the server being able to simply push them whenever it wants, at least not with plain unmodified HTTP.

The naive fix, short polling, has the client ask again and again on a fixed interval, every few seconds, whether anything new exists. It works, and it needs no special infrastructure, but it wastes enormous numbers of requests on a plain no answer, and it makes updates only as fast as the polling interval, never faster.

It is worth being precise about why this limitation exists in the first place: HTTP was designed around documents being requested, not around ongoing conversations, and every mechanism covered in this topic is really a way of bending that document-request model, or in the case of WebSockets, stepping outside it entirely, to support an ongoing conversation instead.

This same limitation is why the earliest real-time-feeling web features, things like an inbox unread count, were built on short polling out of necessity rather than choice, since long polling, server-sent events, and WebSockets each arrived later as progressively better answers to the same underlying gap in plain HTTP.
2. Long Polling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396523086-34304428.png
blocks.alt: Long polling holds the request open on the server until an update is ready, avoiding most of the wasted no-answer requests

blocks.content: Long polling changes one thing about short polling that matters a great deal: instead of answering immediately with no, the server holds the request open, without responding, until either an update becomes available or a timeout is reached. The moment an update is ready, the server responds immediately, the client processes it, and immediately opens another long-poll request to wait for the next one.

This gets updates to the client close to as fast as they happen, since the server responds the instant something is ready rather than waiting for the client next scheduled check-in, while still working over plain HTTP with no special protocol or infrastructure needed beyond the willingness to hold a request open for a while.

Long polling also plays reasonably well with existing HTTP infrastructure, proxies, load balancers, and firewalls that were only ever designed to understand ordinary requests and responses, which is exactly why it remained a popular fallback for years in environments where a raw WebSocket connection might get blocked or misbehave somewhere along the network path.
2.1 The Timeout Is Doing Real Work
blocks.text: 2.1 The Timeout Is Doing Real Work

blocks.content: The timeout on a long-poll request is not just a safety net, it is load-bearing for the whole approach. Without one, a request with genuinely nothing to report would hang open forever, tying up a server resource indefinitely and giving the client no signal that anything is even still working.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285833731-613545634.png
blocks.alt: A long-poll request either resolves early with real data or resolves empty at a timeout, prompting the client to open a fresh one

blocks.title: Picking a timeout value
blocks.content: Too short and the approach degrades back toward wasteful short polling, since most requests time out with nothing to report. Too long and a request sits open consuming a server-side resource, like a thread or a connection slot, for longer than is comfortable. Most systems land somewhere between twenty and sixty seconds.

It is also worth handling the empty timeout response as a completely normal, expected outcome on the client side rather than an error. A client that treats every empty response as a failure and backs off aggressively can end up polling far less often than intended, quietly degrading the responsiveness the whole approach was meant to provide.
3. WebSockets
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285835269-640909910.png
blocks.alt: A WebSocket connection starts as an HTTP request, upgrades to a persistent connection, and then either side can send messages at any time

blocks.content: A WebSocket is a genuinely different mechanism: a single, long-lived, full-duplex connection between client and server, opened once and kept open, over which either side can send a message to the other at any moment with no need to open a new request first. Once the connection is established there is no more request-response ceremony, just messages flowing in either direction whenever there is something to send.

GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

blocks.content: That handshake is how a WebSocket connection begins: an ordinary HTTP request asking to upgrade the connection, and a server response agreeing, after which the same underlying network connection stops speaking HTTP and starts speaking the WebSocket protocol instead, staying open for as long as both sides want it to.

It is worth noting the protocol identifier itself changes too, a WebSocket connection is addressed with ws colon or wss colon for the encrypted version, rather than http or https, even though the connection began life as an ordinary HTTP request before the upgrade completed.

It is worth remembering that a WebSocket only defines how messages get sent back and forth, not what those messages mean. The application layer on both ends still has to agree on a message format, typically JSON with a type field indicating what kind of event it represents, since the protocol itself is deliberately just a transport.
3.1 Load Balancers Need To Know About This
blocks.text: 3.1 Load Balancers Need To Know About This

blocks.content: An ordinary HTTP load balancer is used to routing each independent request wherever makes sense at that moment, since one request has no relationship to the next. A WebSocket connection breaks that assumption: once a client is upgraded and connected to a specific server, every subsequent message over that same connection has to keep reaching that same server, since the connection itself lives there.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285837363-19855050.png
blocks.alt: A load balancer has to pin a client to the same backend server for the lifetime of a WebSocket connection rather than routing freely per request

blocks.title: This is called sticky routing
blocks.content: Getting this wrong means a load balancer trying to route a message to a server that has no idea who the client is, since the actual open socket lives on a different server entirely. Sticky routing at the load balancer, combined with the pub or sub backplane covered earlier for cross-server messages, is the standard combination that makes this work correctly at scale.

Some architectures sidestep sticky routing entirely by terminating WebSocket connections at a dedicated, horizontally scaled connection-handling layer that itself talks to backend services over ordinary stateless requests or an internal message queue, keeping the tricky long-lived-connection concerns isolated to one purpose-built layer instead of spread across every backend service.

Most managed load balancer products explicitly document their WebSocket support and any sticky session configuration needed to enable it, which is worth checking early when choosing infrastructure for a real-time feature rather than discovering a gap in support after the design is otherwise finished.
4. Comparing Overhead

Long polling reopens a new HTTP request every single time an update is delivered, and every HTTP request carries its own overhead: headers, and depending on the setup, a new connection or at least a new request cycle on an existing one. Under frequent updates, that repeated overhead adds up to real, measurable cost on both the client and the server.

A WebSocket pays a small one-time cost to open the connection and then essentially no per-message overhead beyond the message content itself, since there is no repeated request cycle at all. For anything with frequent, bidirectional updates, a chat application being the clearest example, this difference is not a minor optimization, it is often the deciding factor between the two approaches.

Battery and mobile data usage follow the same pattern as server-side overhead. Repeatedly opening new HTTP requests on a mobile device costs more radio and battery activity than keeping one connection open and idle between messages, which is worth remembering for any real-time feature that needs to run well on phones over a cellular connection.
4.1 A Worked Numeric Example

Say a chat feature sends an average of one message every two seconds per active conversation, and ten thousand conversations are active at once. With long polling, every single message delivery means closing one request and opening a new one, roughly five thousand new HTTP request cycles per second across the system, each carrying its own headers and connection overhead.

With WebSockets, those same ten thousand conversations correspond to ten thousand connections that were opened once and stay open, and delivering a message means writing a small frame onto an already-open socket, no new connection, no repeated headers, no request cycle at all. The gap between these two only grows as message frequency increases, which is exactly why chat products lean on WebSockets rather than long polling once they have any meaningful scale.

It is worth running through a similar calculation for whatever specific system is actually being designed, rather than trusting this example number directly, since the crossover point where WebSockets clearly win shifts with message frequency, payload size, and how expensive a new HTTP request cycle is on the specific infrastructure in question.

Server CPU spent parsing repeated HTTP headers and managing repeated connection setup is often the less obvious cost compared to raw bandwidth, and it is the one that tends to surprise teams first when a long-polling based feature grows well beyond its original expected scale.
5. Server-Sent Events As A Middle Ground
blocks.text: 5. Server-Sent Events As A Middle Ground

blocks.content: Server-sent events offer a simpler option for the common case where only the server ever needs to push data and the client never needs to send anything back over the same channel. It is a single long-lived HTTP response that the server keeps writing new events into over time, using an ordinary HTTP connection with no special upgrade handshake, and the browser has built-in support for automatically reconnecting if the connection drops.

This is a meaningfully simpler thing to build and operate than a full WebSocket when the use case is genuinely one-directional, a live news ticker or a progress indicator being good examples, and reaching for the full complexity of WebSockets for a purely one-way stream is worth questioning when server-sent events would do the job with less moving infrastructure.

One real limitation worth naming is that some older proxies and browsers historically capped the number of simultaneous connections to a single domain, which could bite an application opening several independent server-sent event streams to the same origin at once. This is far less of a concern with modern browsers and HTTP versions, but is worth a quick check for any environment with unusual or legacy client requirements.
5.1 What Server-Sent Events Look Like In Code
blocks.text: 5.1 What Server-Sent Events Look Like In Code

blocks.content: The appeal of server-sent events shows up clearly once you see how little code is needed on the client side, since the browser handles the connection, the parsing, and even automatic reconnection natively, with no custom client library required at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285839095-418841337.png
blocks.alt: A single open HTTP request carries a continuous stream of named events from server to client with no request repeated for each one

blocks.content: Browser support for server-sent events is also close to universal, and unlike a raw WebSocket, it plays more naturally with existing HTTP infrastructure like proxies and load balancers, since it never leaves the HTTP protocol in the first place, which is a genuine operational advantage worth weighing against WebSockets full-duplex capability that server-sent events simply do not need for a one-way stream.
6. Scaling Persistent Connections

Every open WebSocket or long-poll connection holds resources on the server for as long as it is open, which is a fundamentally different scaling shape than ordinary stateless HTTP requests that come and go in milliseconds. A server holding a hundred thousand open WebSocket connections has to keep that many sockets and their associated memory alive simultaneously, and the practical connection limit per server becomes a real capacity number to plan around.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396523087-831208024.png
blocks.alt: Two clients connected to two different servers still need to reach each other, which requires a shared pub or sub backplane connecting the servers

blocks.content: This gets harder the moment more than one server is involved, since a message meant for a client connected to server two might originate from a client connected to server one, and the two servers have no way to reach each other directly. The standard fix is a shared pub or sub backplane sitting behind all the servers: any server can publish a message to it, and every other server subscribed to the relevant channel receives it and forwards it to whichever of its own locally connected clients need it.

Capacity planning for a real-time system therefore looks noticeably different from planning for a stateless HTTP service. The relevant number is not just requests per second, it is concurrent open connections, and the two scale very differently: a service can have low request throughput but an enormous number of idle, currently-open connections at the same time.
6.1 Thread-Per-Connection Does Not Scale Far

An older, simpler server design dedicates one operating system thread to each open connection, which is easy to reason about but runs into trouble quickly at real scale, since threads are relatively heavyweight and an operating system scheduling tens of thousands of them starts spending a meaningful fraction of its time just managing the threads rather than doing useful work.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285843052-227881994.png
blocks.alt: Dedicating one thread per open connection runs into memory and scheduling overhead long before reaching the connection counts a real-time system needs

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785285844630-732000757.png
blocks.alt: An event-driven server handles many open sockets on a small number of threads, avoiding the per-connection thread overhead entirely

blocks.content: This is exactly why high-connection-count real-time servers are almost always built on an event-driven, non-blocking model instead, the same architectural idea covered in the concurrency versus parallelism topic: a small number of threads efficiently handling many concurrent connections, rather than one thread tied up per connection regardless of whether that connection currently has anything to do.

This is a direct, practical application of the concurrency concepts covered elsewhere in this section: a real-time server is overwhelmingly I/O bound, spending almost all of its time waiting on network activity across many connections rather than computing, which is precisely the shape of workload an event-driven, single or few-threaded design handles best.
6.2 Idle Connections Still Cost Something

Even in a well-built event-driven server, every open connection, whether it currently has anything to send or not, still occupies a file descriptor and a small amount of tracked state. A server planning for a million concurrent connections has to raise operating system limits on open file descriptors specifically, since the default limits on most systems are set far lower than that and will start rejecting new connections long before the intended capacity is reached.

blocks.title: A common first production surprise
blocks.content: Hitting an operating system file descriptor limit is one of the most common first surprises teams run into when a real-time feature grows past its initial testing scale, and it is worth checking and raising deliberately well before it becomes an incident.

Memory per connection matters too, even a small amount of tracked state per connection, like buffers or session metadata, multiplies into a real total once millions of connections are open at once, which is worth estimating explicitly during capacity planning rather than discovered after the fact when a server starts running low on memory under normal expected load.
7. Reconnection And Missed Messages

Any persistent connection eventually drops, a phone loses signal, a laptop goes to sleep, a server restarts during a deployment, and a robust real-time system has to treat this as a routine event rather than an edge case. The client needs reconnection logic, and the harder problem is recovering whatever messages were sent during the gap while the connection was down.

blocks.title: The common fix
blocks.content: Attaching an increasing sequence number or a timestamp to each message lets a reconnecting client tell the server the last one it successfully received, so the server can replay anything sent since then rather than the client silently missing messages that arrived during the disconnected window.

Heartbeat messages, small periodic pings sent over an otherwise idle connection, are the other common piece of this puzzle, letting both sides detect a silently dead connection, one that looks open but is no longer actually delivering data, well before a real message would have exposed the problem.

Client-side reconnection logic itself deserves a moment of care: reconnecting instantly and repeatedly against a server that is down, or overwhelmed, just adds load to an already struggling system. An exponential backoff between reconnection attempts, waiting a little longer each time up to some cap, is the standard way to reconnect promptly when possible without piling on during an outage.
8. Common Anti-Patterns

["Reaching for short polling with an aggressive interval when long polling or a push-based approach would cut both latency and load.","Building a full WebSocket implementation for a purely one-directional stream that server-sent events would handle more simply.","Scaling a WebSocket service across multiple servers with no shared backplane, so clients connected to different servers cannot reach each other.","Assuming a persistent connection never drops and skipping reconnection and missed-message handling entirely."]
items: Reaching for short polling with an aggressive interval when long polling or a push-based approach would cut both latency and load.
Building a full WebSocket implementation for a purely one-directional stream that server-sent events would handle more simply.
Scaling a WebSocket service across multiple servers with no shared backplane, so clients connected to different servers cannot reach each other.
Assuming a persistent connection never drops and skipping reconnection and missed-message handling entirely.

blocks.content: A quieter version of the last anti-pattern is worth calling out on its own: even with a backplane in place, forgetting to handle the case where a server crashes while holding open connections, leaving those clients disconnected with no automatic reroute, silently drops a slice of users until their client-side reconnection logic notices and reconnects to a healthy server.
9. Real-World Examples

{"headers":["Use case","Common approach"],"rows":[["Chat applications","WebSockets, for low-latency, frequent, bidirectional messages"],["Live sports scores or stock tickers","Server-sent events or long polling, since the client rarely needs to send anything back"],["Collaborative document editing","WebSockets, needing fast bidirectional updates as multiple people type at once"],["Legacy or constrained environments","Long polling, when WebSocket support or infrastructure is not available"]]}

Multiplayer games sit at the extreme end of this spectrum, needing not just a persistent connection but often a specialized transport built on top of UDP rather than TCP entirely, trading guaranteed delivery for lower latency, since a slightly stale position update that arrives fast is more useful than a perfectly reliable one that arrives late.
9.1 A Practical Decision Guide

{"headers":["Situation","Reach for"],"rows":[["Frequent updates in both directions","WebSockets"],["Server-only updates, client never sends back","Server-sent events"],["Infrequent updates, simplicity matters more than latency","Long polling"],["Environment where WebSocket support is uncertain","Long polling as a fallback"]]}

blocks.title: Fallback chains are common in practice
blocks.content: Many production real-time libraries attempt a WebSocket connection first and automatically fall back to long polling if the upgrade fails for any reason, giving most clients the better experience while still working everywhere.

None of these situations are perfectly clean in practice, and real products often mix approaches across different features: a chat panel using WebSockets while a separate notification badge on the same page updates through simple polling, since the two features have genuinely different freshness and bidirectionality needs even though they live in the same application.
10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: This topic comes up whenever a design needs anything resembling real-time behavior, and a strong answer names the actual requirement, bidirectional versus one-way, frequency of updates, number of expected concurrent connections, before picking a mechanism. Defaulting straight to WebSockets for a simple one-way notification feed misses server-sent events as the simpler, equally valid option.

It is also worth being ready to discuss the scaling side directly: how connections are distributed across servers, what happens when a server holding thousands of connections needs to restart, and how a message gets from one server to a client connected to a different one. That operational depth is what separates a surface-level answer from one that shows real experience running this kind of system.
Polling asks again and again. Long polling waits patiently for one answer. A WebSocket just leaves the line open.
10.1 A Common Follow-Up Question

A frequent follow-up asks how you would test that real-time delivery is actually working correctly in production, not just in a demo. A grounded answer mentions tracking end-to-end delivery latency and a missed-message rate as real monitored metrics, the same way any other critical path would be monitored, rather than treating real-time delivery as something that either obviously works or obviously does not.

blocks.title: Why this resonates with interviewers
blocks.content: Treating a WebSocket or long-polling layer as just another piece of infrastructure that needs monitoring, not a magic always-on feature, is exactly the operational maturity that distinguishes a strong system design answer from a purely theoretical one.

A second common follow-up asks how authentication works for a connection that is opened once and stays open for hours, unlike a per-request token that gets checked on every single call. The typical answer validates identity once during the initial handshake, then relies on the connection itself being the proof of that identity for its lifetime, with a separate mechanism to forcibly close a connection if that identity needs to be revoked mid-session.

None of these four options, short polling, long polling, server-sent events, and WebSockets, is obsolete. Each remains the right tool in specific circumstances, and recognizing which circumstance you are actually in matters more than defaulting to whichever one feels most modern.
Key Takeaways

["Short polling is simple but wasteful; long polling holds the request open to reduce that waste while still using plain HTTP.","WebSockets provide a persistent, full-duplex connection with minimal per-message overhead after a one-time handshake.","Server-sent events are a simpler middle ground for purely one-directional server-to-client streams.","Persistent connections are held resources, and scaling them across multiple servers needs a shared pub or sub backplane.","Reconnection and missed-message recovery need explicit handling since any persistent connection can and will eventually drop."]
items: Short polling is simple but wasteful; long polling holds the request open to reduce that waste while still using plain HTTP.
WebSockets provide a persistent, full-duplex connection with minimal per-message overhead after a one-time handshake.
Server-sent events are a simpler middle ground for purely one-directional server-to-client streams.
Persistent connections are held resources, and scaling them across multiple servers needs a shared pub or sub backplane.
Reconnection and missed-message recovery need explicit handling since any persistent connection can and will eventually drop.
